rows.description: My friend fell and I help him up and ask "are you okay?" I feel a warm ache for him. Wise adults notice and say "that was kind". A child who cares about others is learning to read feelings.
My parent notices I helped set the table and says "thank you, that was a big help". I feel important. Small chores with real thanks build a sense of being useful, without turning help into payment.
My friend helped me find my lost shoe and I feel relieved and happy. I say "thank you". Being helped by a peer teaches that friends look out for each other, and I plan to help back.
I beg my parents for something I saw in an ad and they refuse. I feel angry and it seems unfair. Understanding their limits and offering to save for it myself shows growing maturity.
My parent buys me something after I waited patiently. It feels extra special. Learning to wait makes me value things and understand the effort behind them.
I love watching a YouTuber who seems to have a perfect life. Admiration can inspire me, but I remember that videos are edited and nobody's real life is only fun.
All my friends have the new branded shoes and I feel left out. Wanting to fit in is human. I can ask myself whether friendship depends on shoes, and talk to my parents honestly.
My friends tell scary stories about police and I get nervous. I can ask parents what police really do, and learn that a good officer helps children.
I see a policeman in uniform and feel respect and slight fear. Police exist to keep people safe; I can learn that I may ask them for help if I am lost or in trouble.
I learn to stop at red lights and cross at zebra crossings. Rules keep everyone safe, and I remind adults politely if they break them.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior seems to dislike me and speaks against me in the team. I feel stung. I ask myself what they may have felt from my behaviour, speak with them openly, and hold my standards without needing everyone to like me.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior treats every word of mine as gospel and I feel flattered and slightly uncomfortable. I share my mistakes, encourage them to think for themselves, and avoid using their admiration to gain control.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior who once admired me sees my mistake and turns cold. I feel exposed. I own the error without fuss, let them adjust their picture of me, and value being trusted as real over being admired as perfect.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior keeps running to me for every decision and I feel needed and drained. I ask them what they think, gently step back, and show that my job is to grow their judgment, not their reliance.
Riders at the tea stall share safe routes, warn about bad customers and help with a broken bike. I feel belonging. Wise: nurture this network and use it to ask for better terms together.

The app cuts my per-trip rate and blocks my ID with no human to speak to. I feel powerless against an algorithm. Wise: keep screenshots, join a workers' group, track real earnings after fuel, and build other income.

A customer offers water and says "take care on the road". A tiny kindness makes my day. Wise: accept it warmly and pass it on. Harmful: none; but do not let strangers' moods decide my self-worth either way.

I hide from relatives that I deliver food because they see it as low status. I feel a private sting. Wise: honest work is nothing to be ashamed of; explain my plan and timeline. Harmful: lying and drifting into stagnation.
A friend gave me an expensive gift and I feel I must give back. Gifts should not be a debt. I thank her, and give something within my means when I can. Feeling pressured is a sign to talk openly.
An older person gives me presents and asks me to keep it secret. Gifts with secrets are a warning. I tell my parents right away and stay away. It is never my fault and telling is always right.
I got a nice gift and my friend looks unhappy. I understand she may feel left out. I share or include her, but I do not need to hide my joy. Bragging is the part to avoid.
A friend gives me a small handmade card and I feel warm. I say thank you and mean it. The thought counts more than the price. Comparing it with fancier gifts spoils the joy.
